message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This proposal is built on our own trading history, not just competitor benchmarking, and that is what makes me confident in it. The key question with any rate rise is price sensitivity, and we have a direct test: when we raised the weekend rate by £10 last June, weekend occupancy went up, from 81% to 89%, the following month. Combined with a value-for-money score of 8.4, the best in our set, and rates £20 to £35 below competitors, everything points the same way. The revenue estimate is deliberately conservative: it assumes no occupancy gain and puts no value at all on the extra Friday and Sunday nights that the two-night minimum will generate, so £204,000 is a floor rather than a target. We have also built in a clear monitoring trigger, so if occupancy does dip we will see it within a month and can respond. Corporate and group commitments are protected. I think this is a well-evidenced, low-risk change that brings our pricing into line with the quality of the hotel.
</author>

<document>
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.
</document>
response:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure, Harbourside Hotel

**Overall:** The underlying idea is plausible. Harbourside is priced below its competitive set, and Saturdays sell out often. But the paper's key evidence doesn't show what it claims. The revenue figure is built on the wrong room count, and the two-night minimum clashes with the paper's own data on wedding guests. The estimate is not a floor: it assumes the main risk away rather than allowing for it.

## Major issues

### 1. The June-to-July comparison measures the season, not the price

Section 3 compares July with June and finds occupancy rose after the £10 increase. But Table 1 shows July is *always* one of the strongest months. The paper itself credits the harbour festival and school holidays. Weekend occupancy in 2025 went:

> May 85% → **Jun 81%** → **Jul 89%** → Aug 93% → Sep 88%

A rise from June to July is what you'd expect at any price. Nothing here separates the effect of the price from the effect of the season. What would test it:

- July 2025 compared with July 2024 (year on year, at the old and new rates);
- pick-up pace, meaning bookings made after the change compared with the same booking window the previous year;
- a check on whether the increase actually reached bookings, since much of July would already have been booked at £135 before the late-June change.

As written, the data cannot support the claim that guests "are not price sensitive," and nothing at all supports the idea that the increase "reinforced our positioning." Notably, the paper's own monitoring plan in section 6 uses the right method, comparing against the same weeks in 2025. Section 3 should apply the same standard.

The value-for-money score of 8.4 is also weak evidence. It was measured at £135–£145. A high value score at a low price may simply *reflect* the low price. It doesn't show that guests would rate the hotel the same at £165.

### 2. The room count is wrong, so the headline figure is too high

Section 2 says the hotel has **112 rooms**, but section 5 uses **124**.

| Rooms | × 104 nights × 79% × £20 |
|---|---|
| 124 (as used) | £203,800 |
| **112 (as stated)** | **£184,000** |

Even £184,000 is an upper bound, for these reasons:

- **Only BAR bookings get the increase.** Corporate rates, contracted groups, packages, and probably the wedding blocks (38% of Saturdays) won't pay the new rate.
- **OTA commission** takes a share of every pound on bookings made through online agencies.
- **VAT.** If £145 and £165 are VAT-inclusive, the £20 is about £16.67 net.
- **Bookings already on the books.** Stays from 1 June that were booked before 15 May keep the old rate. The busy summer months will be heavily pre-booked, so the gain in 2026 will be well below a full year's figure.

Before going to the GM, the paper should restate the figure on BAR room nights only, net of commission and VAT.

### 3. The two-night minimum works against the paper's own wedding data

Section 4 says 38% of Saturday room bookings are wedding guests who arrive on Saturday and leave on Sunday. A two-night minimum would require these guests to pay for a night they don't want, or send them to other hotels. That could also damage the relationship with Quayside Hall.

On top of that:

- **Most Saturdays don't sell out.** On the 21 Saturdays that didn't sell out in 2025, the minimum turns away one-night guests who would otherwise have filled empty rooms.
- **The "conversion" is assumed, not shown.** The paper gives no data on how many single-night guests would book a second night rather than go elsewhere.

The minimum could easily *lower* Saturday occupancy. That makes the decision not to quantify it the opposite of conservative.

### 4. "Conservative" and "a floor" aren't justified

The estimate assumes occupancy holds at 2025 levels. But the realistic risk is occupancy *falling*, from both the price rise and the minimum stay. Assuming no fall is a central or optimistic case, not a prudent one. "At least £204,000" in section 7 should be replaced with a range.

It would help to give a break-even figure instead. Raising the rate from £145 to £165 increases revenue as long as weekend occupancy falls by less than about **12% of its current level**. At 79% average occupancy, that's a drop of about **9.5 points**, to about 69.5%. Once the lost restaurant, bar and other spend from each empty room is included, the margin is smaller.

## Other issues

- **One flat rate for the whole year:** January (62%) and July (89%) get the same £20 increase. A rise is easiest to justify on high-demand dates and hardest in winter. A seasonal or demand-based rate would capture most of the gain with less risk. The same applies to the minimum stay: use it on dates when demand is high, not every Saturday.
- **The monitoring trigger lags:** The direction is right, comparing with 2025, but "a month falls more than five points below" is only seen after the month ends. By then, later months are already being booked at the new rate and under the minimum-stay rule. A trigger on weekly pick-up pace for the next 60–90 days would give earlier warning.
- **Group protection is narrower than described:** The paper only honours groups "already contracted." Future wedding blocks aren't covered. The paper should say whether they'll get a group rate and an exemption from the minimum stay.
- **"Recovered strongly since 2023":** No data is given for this.
- **What's correct:** The "£20 to £35 below" competitor gap is right (£145 against £165–£180), and the arithmetic in section 5 is right for 124 rooms.

## On your description specifically

- **"A direct test":** It isn't one. The June-to-July change is driven by the season, as your own table shows.
- **"Assumes no occupancy gain":** True, but the risk being left out is occupancy *loss*.
- **"£204,000 is a floor":** It isn't. It uses 12 rooms too many and counts every room night as BAR.
- **"Corporate and group commitments are protected":** Only existing contracts are protected. Wedding guests, the biggest Saturday segment, are exposed to the minimum stay.

## Suggested changes

1. Replace the June-to-July evidence with a year-on-year and pick-up analysis, or drop the claim that guests aren't price sensitive.
2. Correct the room count, and restate the revenue on BAR nights only, net of commission and VAT. Show a range and the break-even occupancy.
3. Exempt wedding blocks from the minimum stay, or limit it to high-demand dates, and estimate the likely turn-aways.
4. Consider seasonal pricing rather than a flat £20 increase.
5. Add a forward-looking pick-up trigger alongside the monthly occupancy review.

Revised this way, the proposal would probably still recommend a rate increase. The case would be accurate, and the owners could rely on the numbers.
